qt: to the Commission Aurélia Beigneux (ID) Subject:

Most beekeepers sell the honey they produce directly to packagers in a long supply chain. Honey consumption is currently falling due to high food inflation. Sales via long supply chains in 2023 were disastrous: the packagers did not buy enough and the prices offered to beekeepers fell by 50%. The European Anti-Fraud Office has also uncovered a major fraud: 30% of this honey is apparently adulterated and composed of a simple artificial mixture of fructose and glucose, without the intervention of bees. Such conduct misleads consumers and puts them at risk. In this context: 1.
What action does the Commission plan to take, and in what timeframe, to support the beekeeping sector?
Does the Commission intend to step up checks on laboratories responsible for analysing imported honey, with a view to increasing transparency and tackling unfair foreign competition?
at: (English version) to the Commission Aurélia Beigneux (ID) (2 February 2024) Subject: Crisis in beekeeping Most beekeepers sell the honey they produce directly to packagers in a long supply chain. Honey consumption is currently falling due to high food inflation. Sales via long supply chains in 2023 were disastrous: the packagers did not buy enough and the prices offered to beekeepers fell by 50%. The European Anti-Fraud Office has also uncovered a major fraud: 30% of this honey is apparently adulterated and composed of a simple artificial mixture of fructose and glucose, without the intervention of bees. Such conduct misleads consumers and puts them at risk. In this context: 1.
What action does the Commission plan to take, and in what timeframe, to support the beekeeping sector?
Does the Commission intend to step up checks on laboratories responsible for analysing imported honey, with a view to increasing transparency and tackling unfair foreign competition?

(1 March 2024) The Union supports beekeeping through apiculture interventions which are a mandatory part of the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) Strategic Plans implemented by Member States. The dedicated EU annual budget of EUR 60 million is at least doubled with national co-financing. Member States can also increase their co-financing up to 70% to finance up to seven interventions aimed at improving the general conditions of production and marketing of apiculture products. Other CAP instruments can also be used to address the needs of the sector. The 2021-2022 EU-wide investigation on imported honey (1) showed that a significant part of the samples tested was suspected of adulteration with sugar and thus non-compliant with the requirements of the EU Honey Directive (2). Although it is clear that not every suspected honey sample is a case of intentional adulteration, the Commission has taken these results very seriously. Already in 2022, EU import requirements were reinforced by placing an authenticity requirement for exporting countries in honey import certificates (3). A recent amendment to Delegated Regulation (EU) 2022/2292 (4) will make the import of honey possible only from establishments listed in accordance with the Official Controls Regulation (EU) 2017/625 (5). Moreover, to increase the capabilities of Member States’ control authorities to detect honey fraud, the Commission launched in 2023 a project addressing the need for validated methods of analysis that are fit-for-purpose to detect new types of sugar-based adulterants used in honey. Finally, the Honourable Member may be aware of the political agreement reached by the co-legislators on 30 January 2024 on the review of the Honey Directive, including new provisions to support fight against fraud.
